title: How to Pick a Fight You Planned to Win
documentTitle: Epic Games v. Apple — Tim Sweeney Letter on Fortnite Payments (Exhibit G)
excerptForBlog: I'm writing to tell you that Epic will no longer adhere to Apple's payment processing restrictions. Today, Epic is launching Epic direct payments in Fortnite on iOS, offering customers the choice of paying in-app through Epic direct payments or through Apple payments, and passing on the savings of Epic direct payments to customers in the form of lower prices. We choose to follow this path in the firm belief that history and law are on our side. Smartphones are essential computing devices that people use to live their lives and conduct their business. Apple's position that its manufacture of a device gives it free rein to control, restrict, and tax commerce by consumers and creative expression by developers is repugnant to the principles of a free society. Henceforth, all versions of Fortnite that Epic submits to the App Store will contain these two payment options, side by side, for customers to choose among. We hope that Apple will reflect on its platform restrictions and begin to make historic changes that bring to the world's billion iOS consumers the rights and freedoms enjoyed on the world's leading open computing platforms including Windows and macOS. If Apple chooses instead to take punitive action by blocking consumer access to Fortnite or forthcoming updates, then Epic will, regrettably, be in conflict with Apple on a multitude of fronts - creative, technical, business, and legal - for so long as it takes to bring about change, if necessary for many years.

sourceCase: Epic Games, Inc. v. Apple Inc.
lessonTitle: How to Pick a Fight You Planned to Win
pullQuote: When you deliberately break a powerful partner's rules, the letter you send isn't a negotiation — it's the opening statement of a lawsuit you've already prepared.
leadershipTraits: willing to absorb short-term losses for structural change
situation: On August 13, 2020, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney sent this letter to Apple, announcing that Fortnite on iOS was launching its own payment option in direct violation of App Store rules. He sent it the same day the change went live. This was not a proposal or a grievance. It was a notification — delivered after the action was already taken.
insight:
Sweeney's real move is a platform jailbreak attempt, executed through deliberate rule-breaking rather than lobbying or litigation. He knew Apple would remove Fortnite. That removal was the point. The letter signals that Epic pre-accepted the consequences: 'Epic will... be in conflict with Apple on a multitude of fronts — creative, technical, business, and legal — for so long as it takes.' This is a classic two-front strategy — force a public confrontation that turns a private contract dispute into a broad antitrust argument. The phrase 'history and law are on our side' shows Epic was betting the legal route was more valuable than the distribution it was about to lose.

The hidden cost-benefit: Apple's 30% fee was Epic's platform tax. Epic calculated that owning the payment relationship — and the precedent — was worth more than staying on the App Store quietly. Whether that math worked is context this single document cannot answer.
application: Before you violate a powerful partner's terms, write out every retaliation scenario and confirm you have a response for each one. Sweeney explicitly names the retaliation he expected ('blocking consumer access') and commits to fighting it. If you cannot name the worst case and honestly say you can survive it, you are not ready to pick the fight.
